newsitem.title: JAPAN: Dollar seen facing resistance above 116.50 yen.
newsitem.headline: Dollar seen facing resistance above 116.50 yen.

text.p: The dollar is likely to be well-supported in Asia on Wednesday, but it may be capped against the yen by exporter offers above 116.50 yen.
The U.S. currency is underpinned by solid bids around 115.50 yen, a trust bank trader said.
The dollar is also likely to remain well-bid versus the mark amid continuing uncertainty about the future of a single European currency, dealers said.
"Unless the EU decides to postpone monetary union, downward pressure on the mark should persist," a trader at a city bank said.
The dollar ended marginally higher in Tuesday's New York trade, as uncertainty over a German plan to revalue gold reserves and speculation about a weak single European currency weighed on the mark.

Germany's Finance Minister Theo Waigel said on Tuesday that he had reached a "good compromise" with Bundesbank President Hans Tietmeyer under which the transfer of gold profits to government coffers would be postponed until 1998.
But Tietmeyer said later in the day that no formal deal had been struck yet but the two sides were close to an agreement.
The dollar may be capped against the mark by profit-taking pressure above Tuesday's Tokyo high of around 1.7333 marks, dealers said.
There is also talk of selling interest by hedge funds around 1.7325 marks, dealers said.
Meanwhile, the mark is likely to remain under downward pressure against the yen, dealers said.
"If some speculative selling emerges in mark/yen, we may see a dip to around 66.30 yen," the city bank trader said.
The mark stood at around 67.19 yen in late New York on Tuesday.
Tokyo operators are closely watching Friday's release of U.S. employment data for May.
If a stronger-than-expected jobs data leads to expectations of a rise in U.S. interest rates, the dollar could break above its recent trading range, dealers said.
Economists polled by Reuters on Monday predicted on average an increase of 219,000 in new jobs in non-farm payrolls in May.
Dealers also said any remarks about Japanese interest rates by the Japanese government officials could bring about swings in dollar/yen.
